analysis.one_liner: Lets union contracts require workers to join the union, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 27 House Democrats, was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the part of federal labor law (Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act) that lets states pass 'right-to-work' laws, which ban contracts requiring workers to join or pay dues to a union as a condition of keeping their job. If the bill passed, unions and employers in any state could agree to union-security clauses even where state law currently forbids them. It would affect millions of workers in the roughly half of states with right-to-work laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at unionized workplaces in right-to-work states, who under current law can get union representation free of charge without joining or paying dues; unions, which would gain members and dues income and stronger bargaining leverage; and workers generally in those states, where unions argue union-security agreements raise pay and stabilize contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal provision that lets states ban agreements requiring union membership as a condition of employment, overriding state right-to-work laws [S2] [S3].
Allows unions and employers in any state to negotiate union-security clauses, so workers who benefit from union representation would share its cost rather than riding free.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in right-to-work states who prefer not to belong to a union would face joining or paying union fees as a condition of employment. Unions and workers would also pay: unions would have to spend on organizing in states long closed to them, and economists who support right-to-work laws argue such states attract more employers, so some jobs could shift away. Opponents of the bill frame it as taking a choice from individual workers and giving it to union majorities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers who decline to join unions

drawbacks.text: Workers who do not want to belong to a union could be required to join or pay fees to keep their job, replacing individual choice with a contract-level requirement [S2] [S3].

Supporters of right-to-work laws argue these statutes attract employers and that repealing the state option could cost jobs in right-to-work states; the bill also erases a policy choice currently made state by state.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want union representation and stronger contracts, the bill removes a legal barrier that lets others take union gains without paying for them. The real cost falls on workers who prefer not to join, and the bill does nothing to address that conflict except side with the union-majority view. It also does not directly raise anyone's pay; its benefits depend entirely on workers winning and keeping union contracts afterward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman and 15 colleagues introduced the bill on September 5, 2023; it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce that day [S5] [S3].
A total of 26 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote after the referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in right-to-work states keep a labor environment where workers cannot be required to join or pay a union, and nonunion workers in those states keep their individual choice. Unions and their allies gained nothing from the effort.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 15 original cosponsors

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill; it received no committee action after referral

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 5, 2023 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 27 sponsors were House Democrats and no Republicans cosponsored; the Republican-controlled committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would let unions negotiate membership or fee requirements in states that currently ban them, expanding union membership rolls and dues income in roughly half the states. Unions argue the same change raises pay and bargaining power for the workers it covers.

Employers that recruit in right-to-work states would lose the legal environment in which no worker can be required to join or fund a union, and could face union-security clauses at organized workplaces.
